headline: Tech enthusiast finds $12,000 stack of RAM in their garage, totaling 1,920GB DDR4 from an old server
summary: The RAM consists of 30 Samsung 64GB DDR4 ECC registered DIMMs, valued at roughly $400 each, but they are only compatible with server-grade systems like Xeon, Epyc, or Threadripper.
details: A computing enthusiast on Reddit, VastOption8705, shared images of finding 30 sticks of 64GB DDR4-2666 RAM in their garage. This massive haul totals 1,920GB and is estimated to be worth around $12,000.
The Redditor acquired the RAM after being allowed to keep an old server from their workplace. This practice can sometimes save companies recycling fees for old equipment.
The RAM sticks are specifically Samsung 64GB DDR4 ECC registered DIMMs (RDIMMs). These are server-grade modules designed for Intel Xeon, AMD Epyc, or AMD Threadripper platforms.
Unfortunately for consumer PC users, these ECC RDIMMs are both physically and electrically incompatible with standard home creator or gaming PCs, even if the motherboard supports DDR4.

While the $12,000 valuation is based on eBay listings for individual 64GB DDR4-2666 sticks, the original poster's $10K estimate was close. If the original poster is in Australia, AU$10,000 converts to roughly US$7,200.
caption:
A tech enthusiast discovered 1,920GB of DDR4 RAM, valued at up to $12,000, in their garage. It came from an old server they were allowed to keep from work.

A computing enthusiast on Reddit, VastOption8705, shared images of finding 30 sticks of 64GB DDR4-2666 RAM in their garage. This massive haul totals 1,920GB and is estimated to be worth around $12,000.

The Redditor acquired the RAM after being allowed to keep an old server from their workplace. This practice can sometimes save companies recycling fees for old equipment.

The RAM sticks are specifically Samsung 64GB DDR4 ECC registered DIMMs (RDIMMs). These are server-grade modules designed for Intel Xeon, AMD Epyc, or AMD Threadripper platforms.

Unfortunately for consumer PC users, these ECC RDIMMs are both physically and electrically incompatible with standard home creator or gaming PCs, even if the motherboard supports DDR4.

While the $12,000 valuation is based on eBay listings for individual 64GB DDR4-2666 sticks, the original poster's $10K estimate was close. If the original poster is in Australia, AU$10,000 converts to roughly US$7,200.

headline_marked: [[Belgian-Chinese researcher arrested]] for alleged GaN chip trade-secret theft
headline: Belgian-Chinese researcher arrested for alleged GaN chip trade-secret theft
summary: A 52-year-old Belgian-Chinese man was arrested at Brussels airport, suspected of transferring specialized gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductor IP from his employer, BelGaN, to a Chinese firm he allegedly led.
details: A 52-year-old Belgian-Chinese man, identified as H.L., has been arrested in Brussels on suspicion of industrial espionage. He is accused of transferring specialized gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductor intellectual property and trade secrets from Belgian chipmaker BelGaN to China. The arrest occurred on May 10 as he attempted to board a flight to China.

H.L. held a senior research position at the now-defunct BelGaN. Investigators suspect he concurrently led a Chinese chip firm, GanKool, which was developing identical GaN chip technology. GanKool was established months after H.L. joined BelGaN and was financed by a Chinese investment fund.

The espionage allegations emerged during a financial probe into BelGaN's collapse into bankruptcy in summer 2024. Authorities uncovered highly unusual corporate activity during this routine investigation.

Prosecutors suspect managers and H.L. may have actively worked to make BelGaN "disappear" after transferring its proprietary knowledge. This led to further investigations, revealing GanKool's existence and its connections to BelGaN.

H.L. now faces charges including industrial espionage, membership in a criminal organization, misuse of company assets, and unlawful disclosure of business secrets. Investigators also found evidence linking BelGaN's last CEO, a Chinese national, to the same Chinese rival, with a second suspect remaining at large.

This incident highlights intense global competition for semiconductor technology and intellectual property. Similar cases include a former Samsung engineer sentenced for allegedly transferring DRAM technology to Chinese memory maker CXMT.
